analysis.evidence: מִחוּט וְעַד שְׂרוֹךְ נַעַל means “from a thread to a sandal strap.” Abram names two small possessions, then extends his oath to מִכָּל אֲשֶׁר לָךְ, anything belonging to the king.
analysis.morphology: The prefixed preposition מִ־, a form of מִן meaning “from,” introduces the masculine singular absolute noun חוּט.

draft.change: Add the noun שְׂרוֹךְ with its sandal-strap sense and correct the supplied spatial gloss for this occurrence.
draft.definition: A strap used to fasten a sandal.
draft.evidence: Genesis 14:23 pairs a sandal strap with a thread. Isaiah 5:27 identifies its function by saying that no strap of the soldiers’ sandals has come loose.

analysis.evidence: In שְׂרוֹךְ נַעַל, נַעַל identifies the sandal to which the strap belongs. Abram pairs the strap with a thread as he swears to take nothing belonging to the king. Isaiah 5:27 confirms the sense by describing a sandal strap coming loose.
analysis.morphology: Hebrew common noun, masculine singular construct. The following noun נַעַל completes the phrase “the strap of a sandal.”
analysis.sense: A strap used to fasten a sandal.

analysis.evidence: In שְׂרוֹךְ נַעַל, “the strap of a sandal,” שְׂרוֹךְ names the strap and נַעַל identifies the footwear it belongs to. Abram refuses to take even a thread or a sandal strap.
analysis.morphology: Common noun, feminine singular absolute, with no prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: In the oath וְאִם אֶקַּח מִכָּל אֲשֶׁר לָךְ, Abram swears he will accept nothing belonging to the king, even a thread or sandal strap, so the king cannot claim to have made him rich. The oath supplies the negative force.
analysis.morphology: Qal imperfect, first person common singular. The אֶ־ prefix marks first person singular, and the dagesh in ק reflects assimilation of the initial ל of the root.

analysis.evidence: In מִכָּל אֲשֶׁר לָךְ, כָּל denotes all that belongs to Abram’s addressee. The partitive מִן makes the oath a refusal to take anything from that whole, even a thread or a sandal strap.
analysis.morphology: The prefixed preposition מִן loses its נ by assimilation, doubling the כ of כָּל. The noun is masculine singular in the construct state before אֲשֶׁר לָךְ.

analysis.evidence: In מִכָּל אֲשֶׁר לָךְ, “from all that belongs to you,” אֲשֶׁר introduces the relative clause modifying כָּל. The clause expresses possession through לָךְ, “to you.”
analysis.morphology: Indeclinable Hebrew relative particle with no prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: Abram refuses to take anything belonging to the king of Sodom so that the king may never say אֲנִי הֶעֱשַׁרְתִּי אֶת אַבְרָם, “I made Abram rich.” תֹאמַר introduces the king’s imagined words.
analysis.morphology: Qal imperfect, second person masculine singular, with no attached prefix or suffix. The negation לֹא is a separate word.

analysis.evidence: Abram refuses the goods so the king of Sodom cannot say, “I made Abram rich.” The verb הֶעֱשַׁרְתִּי already marks its subject as “I.” The preceding אֲנִי emphasizes the king’s claim to personal credit.
analysis.morphology: Independent first-person common singular personal pronoun, with no prefix or suffix.
analysis.sense: I, as for me (the speaker set apart)

analysis.evidence: Abram refuses the goods so that the king cannot say אֲנִי הֶעֱשַׁרְתִּי אֶת אַבְרָם, “I made Abram rich.” The explicit אֲנִי emphasizes the king’s claim, and אֶת marks Abram as the direct object of the causative verb.
analysis.morphology: Hiphil perfect, first person common singular. The ending ־תִּי marks the subject.
Hebrew direct-object particle with no prefix or suffix.
